lesson.menu_desc: Reporting the meeting to your client -- what was said, and what it meant -- 33 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- What They Told Me
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rodrigo Marques de França | Lesson 9 -- What They Told Me

listenings.text: What I want from an external lawyer after a meeting is three sentences, and I want them in a particular order. What was agreed, what was not agreed, and what you think they will do next. That third one is the one people leave out, because it is the only part that is a judgement rather than a record, and nobody wants to be wrong in writing. I would rather have you wrong in writing than silent. The other thing I ask for, and I have to ask every time, is that you separate what they said from what you concluded. If your note tells me they were unwilling to move on the cap, I need to know whether they said that in those words or whether you watched somebody hesitate for two seconds and drew a conclusion. Both are useful to me. They are not the same thing, and by Thursday nobody remembers which one it was.

There is a sentence I have started using and it has saved me more than once. When I report a meeting now I say, they told me X, and my reading of it is Y. Two clauses, and a visible seam between them. For years I did not do that, and what happened is what happens to everybody. You compress. You take the four things somebody said, plus their tone, plus the fact that they arrived late and looked tired, and you produce one confident sentence: they are not going to sign. And you are usually right, which is the dangerous part, because the one time in eight when you are wrong, nobody can reconstruct how the conclusion was reached, including you. Now I write the two halves separately, and if the second half turns out to be nonsense, at least the first half is still true and the client can work from it.
